en: Table of Contents for the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dachuang Ji of Lingyin:
Discourses on Ascending the Seat; Small-scale Sermons (Xiaocan); Excerpts from Ancient Cases (Jugu); Verses on Ancient Cases (Songgu).
Eulogies, Verses, Minor Buddhist Rituals, and Biographical Sketches;
Recorded Sayings of the Venerable Dàchuān during his tenure at Miaoshèng Chan Monastery in Qìngyuán Prefecture.
Compiled by his disciple Yuǎnkǎi.

In the third month of the tenth year of the Jiading era, the Master entered the mountain gate and said: "The spring mountains layer upon layer in chaotic green; the spring waters ripple in empty azure.
The Gate of Great Liberation stands open; I take your hand and pull you in, yet you will not enter. He let out a shout.
Whether one knows the truth or not, they both come this way. Holding up his staff, he leans it against his left side and says, "Why can neither of them pass?"
Holding up the notice, the Night-Bright Talisman, and the Seal of No-Text: pressing directly and lifting from the side, the Buddhas and Patriarchs beg for their lives.
Letting this one move pass, everyone knows it exists.
Holding up the robe: "Buddha to Buddha, hand to hand—it was not reached; Patriarch to Patriarch, transmitted from one to another—it did not arrive.
Holding up the robe and saying, "As for this here," to shoulder it upon one's back would inevitably tarnish the family tradition.
The Dharma-seat: vast enough to encompass empty space, yet subtle enough to enter the Avīci Hell; it stands out prominently before one’s eyes—how shall one tread upon it?
Behold! Ascending the seat, he holds up the incense and says:

"This single offering of incense is respectfully offered to extend the longevity of the present Emperor, that his sacred person may enjoy ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years."

Next, he held up the incense and said: "I respectfully offer this for the sake of the Lord of the Prefecture, the Palace Aide and Grand Prelate, as well as all the meritorious nobles of the entire prefecture, to increase their years of official service.

He then held up the incense again and said: "This incense is offered hot within the burner, respectfully for the sake of the Great Monk Zeweng, the seventh-generation successor of Yangqi, currently residing at the Celestial Child Jingde Chan Temple on the famous mountain Taibai, to repay the milk of the Dharma."
[The Master] took his seat. He then said: "Opening the forge of a master artisan, wielding the tongs and hammer of the ultimate realm:
dull iron and stubborn copper are cast aside; even the supple gold that bends to the finger must still be struck and tested. A monk asked: "Before Mount Taibai, the Way-fragrance and fruits ripen;
north of the Jing River, auspicious signs appear like the *tánhuā*. As the fourfold assembly gathers before the dais, we pray for your proclamation. The Master said:
"A single moon rises over the sea; how many families ascend the tower? Jian asked, "This is still merely literary expression. What is the one phrase for saving people?
The Master said, "Eight-armed Nātha rolls the embroidered ball. Jian said, "In that case, we see a sleeping tiger again.
The Master said, "The spiritual traces are even further beyond where the monkeys cry. Jian said, "In the past, when Baoshou opened the hall..."
Sansheng brought forward a monk; Baoshou then struck him. What was his intention? The Master said, "There was a lack of strength in his wrist.
The student asked, "Sansheng said, 'If you act as a teacher in this way, you will not only blind the eyes of this monk, but you will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou.
What was his intention? The Master said, "He got eight parts right. The student asked, "In that case..."
"The Three Sages of old and the Master today," the teacher said. "To hear it on the road and repeat it is mere hearsay. He then continued:
"The Buddhas appearing in the world act as if no one else exists; the Patriarchs coming from the West deceive the Hu and hoodwink the Han.

When a single word accords with them, they mistakenly take the bridge of a donkey’s saddle for their father’s chin. When great function flourishes, it is precisely because consciousness is vast and indistinct, with no fundamental basis to rely upon."
One must know that the path beyond is not transmitted by the thousand sages; it involves holding fast and letting go, remaining natural and at ease according to conditions.
At times, atop a solitary peak, one beholds the clouds and the sky; at other times, by the side of an ancient ferry, one muddies the water and blends with the mud.
Thus it may be so, and thus it may not be so. Just as Sanxing said: "Whenever I meet a person, I come forth; once I have come forth, I do not..."
Regarding "Becoming a Person": To promote the Way of transformation, I do not emerge when meeting people; once I emerge, I immediately become a person.
Furthermore, what of it? "The waves at Caoxi are just like this; countless ordinary people are swept away. (The expression of gratitude is not recorded).
Again, it is cited: A monk asked Caoshan, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? Caoshan said, "Caoshan is not as good.
The monk said, "How was it after he appeared in the world? Caoshan said, "Not as good as Caoshan. The Master said, "Do you wish to recognize Caoshan?
Once having followed the affairs of the man from Pan, he also understands how to remain unashamed before others."
Ascending the hall: When the Buddhas appeared in the world and the Patriarchs came from the West, they were met with people’s ridicule and laughter.

Miaosheng stands on the brink of a deep abyss and treads upon thin ice; he knows full well yet deliberately commits these acts. Who is it that ridicules and laughs? (After a long silence) No one understands this meaning; it makes me think of Nanquan.
Ascending the hall: Ten days of rain; today it is clear. This is a public case from many years ago, which I have clearly presented to you all.
If you are beneath an overturned basin [in ignorance], how can you blame this old monk? (He lets out a shout.)
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: A monk visited Cuiyan. Cuiyan said, "When you go out the door, you see Śākyamuni;

when you enter the gate, you meet Maitreya. The monk did not approve. He then visited Mountou Xiu. Xiu asked, "When you go out the door, whom do you see? When you enter the gate, what do you encounter?"
The monk then attained enlightenment. The Master said, "Cuiyan labors but gains no merit; Master Xiu bestows benefit without expense.
While it is not that this monk lacks enlightenment, the day will come when his tongue is pulled out and he must plow the fields.

Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival: When the obscurations are exhausted, clarity returns to its ultimate limit; the home village is ten thousand eight thousand miles away. Letting go completely from the precipice, the ancient sword stands before the skull.
Ascending the hall at the opening of the furnace: Heishan beats the drum; Xuefeng rolls the ball. In this wondrous victory, one does not strike within such a carriage.
Oil. A pair of hands from the destitute. Two pieces of dead firewood. If you hesitate, it will burn away your face.
Tell me, are the eyebrows of Miaosheng there?

Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient precedent: A monk went to He-lin Monastery and knocked on the door. He-lin asked, "Who is it? The monk replied, "A monk. He-lin said, "Do not say you are a monk;
even if a Buddha were to come, he would not be admitted. The Master remarked, "He-lin’s walls and gates are ten thousand fathoms high; how imposing and orderly they are!
Yet, with a single snap of his fingers by that monk, he immediately hoisted the white flag of surrender."
Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the fourth month: The body of the pure dharma-realm has the face of a donkey and the jaw of a horse;
it fundamentally neither appears nor disappears, yet undergoes ten thousand transformations and a thousand changes. Holding up his staff, he said: "The Old Śākyamuni is coming! He is coming!
If you understand, you will together realize the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-body. If you do not understand, then: 'I now bathe all the Tathāgatas.'"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates—day and night emit light and shake the earth.
[He] let out a shout. "When a single film obscures the eye, illusory flowers fall in confusion."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "Lingyun said, 'For thirty years I have sought a swordsman. What does this mean? The Master replied, "He cannot be deceived.
The monk pressed further, "Several times the leaves fell and then sprouted branches again—what of that? The Master answered, "What sort of thing is that?
The monk continued, "Since first seeing the peach blossoms, how about that? The Master replied, "The nose is straight and the eyes are askew. The monk pressed on.
"Up until now, I have had no further doubts. "Where is it that he has no doubts? He replied, "The heart of a thief is always apprehensive.
He pressed further, "Xuan Sha said, 'How perfectly true! How perfectly true! Yet I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate realization. He replied, [as before].
In joy, they shared the same delight, and the assembly rose again. A Zen practitioner who had just arrived asked about the verse on awakening to the Way upon seeing peach blossoms by Lingyun:
"For thirty years I have sought a swordsman; / Several times the leaves fell and sprouts grew anew.
/ Since the moment I first beheld the peach blossoms, / To this very day, I have no further doubts. Xuan Sha said, "How perfectly true! How perfectly true! I can truly guarantee that you, old man..."
The elder brother has not yet attained thorough penetration. He said: "One person thoroughly penetrates the source of the myriad dharmas; another person grasps the crown of the thousand sages.
Nowadays, everyone is without doubt, yet no one has attained thorough penetration. Furthermore, how can they meet with the ancients?
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited the case of Salt Official (Yanguan) addressing the assembly: "Take empty space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet.
What kind of person can strike it? The assembly was speechless. Nanquan said, "If I had been there at that time, I would have simply told him:
'Old Teacher Wang does not beat this broken drum. The Master said: "Nanquan’s single stroke was indeed perfectly appropriate; yet, it is a pity that the land is vast and the people few."
Rare! Is there anyone here today who will exert themselves for the sake of the assembly?

[The Master] ascends the hall and says: "The single word 'knowledge' is the gateway to all calamities. Killing people and setting fires—arresting them alive—is neither a secret strategy of the present day nor a legal code of antiquity;
it is merely providing a ladder for the thief to climb over the wall and cut through the barrier."
"Who is it? [The Master] ascended the hall and cited National Teacher Yanshou of Gushan, who addressed the assembly: "Under the gate of Gushan, one must not cough.
At that time, a monk coughed once. The Master said, "What are you doing? The monk said, "I have a cold. The Master said, "A cold is fine."
The Master said: "The National Teacher’s command is being carried out; all people throughout the world have their wits blunted and their tongues tied.
Yet, how can one prevent this monk from speaking? Nevertheless, do you wish to recognize this monk? He will not cease until he has reached the banks of the Wu River."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A phrase, no phrase—like a vine leaning against a tree. Cutting through iron, severing nails; water does not borrow a path.
When the tree falls, the vine withers. The old bearded man from the Western Heaven has no whiskers. He tramples to death Yangqi’s three-legged donkey! He gave a shout.
Master Xie Jianshou ascends the hall: The weather is fair, so the roof has been covered; The harvest is ripe, so the grain has been reaped.
Having paid the king’s tax, One beats the belly and sings songs of joy. Master Dongshan was neither within the Buddha-dharma nor within the worldly dharma.
Having passed through the place where the monkeys cry out on Mount Ba, Even an iron heart and liver would break with grief.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Once a monk asked Qianfeng, “The Bhagavāns of the ten directions all enter the single path to nirvāṇa;
I wonder, where does the beginning of that path lie? Qianfeng took his staff, drew a line in front of him, and said, “It is right here. The monk took these words...
He requested instruction from Yunmen. Yunmen said, "The fan leaps and bounds up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra.
A carp of the Eastern Sea, struck once with a stick, pours down rain like an overturned basin. The Master said, "Ganpeak’s ingenuity is exhausted; Zhezong’s comes forth through simplicity."
Yunmen said, "When things reach their extreme, they return. You people have just now come from the Sangha Hall; in a short while, you will go back from the Sangha Hall.
Tell me, where is the beginning of the path? If you follow it and walk along, it is a journey of one hundred and eight thousand miles."
Record of the Chan Monastery of Bodai Guanyin in Qingyuan Prefecture, compiled by the disciple Yuankai. Guanyin Hall:
I have no handle; you have realized perfect penetration. Meeting him unexpectedly—do not let him go.
Ascending the seat, he held up the incense.

Having finished the prayers for the Emperor, he again held up the incense and said: "All people throughout the great earth may agree and approve, yet the Venerable Master Zhe has not yet nodded his head.
This clear principle is difficult to manifest; it is the second tally that scorches the earth and permeates the heavens."
Taking his seat, he said: "The True Dharma Eye was entrusted at Vulture Peak; it was extinguished by the blind donkey of the Three Sages.
Seventeen hundred years have passed until now, yet every one of them has driven a stake into empty space. Do you know this matter? Before sound, it is not sound; after form, it is not form.
A mosquito on an iron ox—there is no place for you to set your beak. The Old Śākyamuni never spoke of it."
Having reached the ultimate summit, how could the Great Being of Perfect Penetration dare to look directly at it with his true eye?
As for the old monks of the world, how could they possibly interpose their words? When I, Layman Jie, arrive here, I cannot help but turn cleverness into clumsiness and suffer scrutiny from others.
If you can examine and discern this, you still do not possess the eye of a patch-robed monk. If you cannot examine and discern it, where then is the eye of a patch-robed monk?
Do not say that the weather at Potalaka is foul; the waves ahead will be even more startling.
Again, it is related: When Nanquan first entered his monastery, the administrative officers and head monks invited him to the abbot’s quarters.
At that time, a monk asked, "When you reside in the abbot’s quarters, with what do you instruct people? Nanquan said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox;
when I rose at dawn, I had lost the fire. The Master [Zhaozhou] said: "It is like a bell hanging from its frame; strike it and it rings. It is like a mirror set upon a stand."
"Things come and he reflects them; why was he pressed by this monk until he lost his composure, forgetting what came before and what followed, and speaking dream upon dream?
Suppose tonight someone were to ask you: 'Master, dwelling in your chamber, with what do you instruct people? To him, you should simply say:"
Having arrived late, he was unaware of the well and the hearth.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The sky is clear and the sun shines; the rain falls and the steps are damp. Even the people on Mount Potalaka are still not straightforward.
To say, 'I enter samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation'—what kind of place is this? He struck the meditation desk.
He struck the staff once. "This rouses ten thousand measures of sorrow in Jiangnan, bringing back a dream from the third watch upon the pillow.
Ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat on the fifteenth day of the seventh month: "The ninety-day summer session is now complete.

If you do not penetrate the Diamond Circle, your eyes will remain askance and your nose straight; if you do not swallow the Thorny Chestnut, you will merely point to your chest and ribs. Thirty years hence, should someone suddenly ask—"
Regarding this ultimate matter, how would you speak?
He ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said: 'If one enters through the gate of Mañjuśrī, even walls, tiles, and rubble will trigger your awakening.'"
If you enter through the gate of Avalokiteśvara, even a frog or an earthworm will trigger your realization.
If you enter through the gate of Samantabhadra, you will reach Potalaka without moving a step. Here, first of all, you must not enter through the gate of Avalokiteśvara.
Why is this? A gem is originally without flaw; carved patterns destroy its virtue.
[The Master] ascended the hall and raised a case: A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is the Mohe Mohe sword? The worthy said, "Dust covers the sandals beneath the bed."
The wind blew his head-cloth off the rack. The Master said, "The ancient worthies responded to circumstances like thunder and lightning;
there was no place for them to settle, no place for them to be understood. Yet, from the standpoint of the gate of the patch-robed monks, this is precisely like a dull blade of lead.
Suppose someone were to ask Baotuo, 'What is the Mohe Mohe Sword? He would simply answer him: 'One-nine, two-nine; when we meet, we do not take out our hands.'"
Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival: The great fire has already flowed westward; a crisp air floats over the thousand mountains. A single wild goose cries out across the autumn river;

the sound of mortars and pestles pounds away at the sorrows of parting. If you understand, then ten thousand li away, in the eighth or ninth month, you are but a single body amidst the northwest wind.
If you do not understand, then take the poem of the Yellow Crane Tower and compose a fine piece of your own upon it, for there is nothing better to do.
On the first day of the tenth month, he ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said: "If you encounter Linji, I will drive a wedge through the crown of your head;
if you meet Deshan, I will beat the marrow out of your bones. You all must not harbor deluded thoughts; each of you return to your quarters to warm yourselves by the fire."
Ascending the hall: Before and after the winter solstice, sand flies and stones run; the Buddhas and Patriarchs hide their tracks. An inch of steel is in hand.
"Going to Potalaka to change the water for the fish. "Yellow silk, young lady; the grandson’s condiment mortar. He lets out a shout.
A brief visit to request the ascent of the hall. He cites the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which says: "Universal Eye wishes to see Samantabhadra, yet cannot find him.
Even after entering meditative concentration three times and surveying the entire trichiliocosm, he still does not see him. He then addresses the Buddha."
The Buddha said, "You need only arise from the stillness of samādhi for a single thought-moment, and you will see.

Thereupon, as soon as Puyan gave rise to a single thought-moment, he indeed saw Samantabhadra riding a six-tusked white elephant, dwelling in mid-air. The Master said: "The sky is clear and bright; the sun of wisdom shines high.
Puyan and Samantabhadra have both succeeded in seeing one another. O Head Seat monks, before you have even given rise to a single thought-moment, you are already wandering through the jewels."
Dhā. You have already met the Great Being of Perfect Penetration. Now tell me: when boarding a great vessel and crossing the whale-waves, what is it like?
You must know that far-off mists and billows harbor a different kind of contemplation.
Ascending the hall, he held his staff horizontally across his chest and said: "The majestic command of a patch-robed monk is sweeping and formidable.
To add a single thread would cause the Dharma to fall into decline in India; to subtract a single thread would lead to a struggle for supremacy here in this land.
Even if one neither adds nor subtracts, it is still like a cold hen standing alone. He struck the ground once with the staff.

Ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat: Śākyamuni, during the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, revealed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

This summer on Mount Potalaka, within these one hundred and twenty days, there are likewise four matters: when hungry, eat; when weary, sleep; when vigorous, practice walking meditation; when hot, fan yourself.
Whether one offers incense or not, a gust of west wind arrives; two or three fallen leaves drift by.
An old acquaintance ascends the hall, and [the Master] cites the discourse of Fenyang to the assembly:
"In the gate of Fenyang, there is a golden-maned lion of Xihe who sits crouched at the entrance, biting to death all who come. What skillful means is there to enter Fenyang’s gate and see him?"

A native of Fenyang, the Master said: "With double moats and double ditches, double fortifications and double encampments, with the front blocked and the rear cleared, one cannot avoid having every limb exposed.
How can this compare to here at Potalaka, where the three gates stand wide open and the abbot’s quarters are left unlocked? Those who come may come as they please;
those who wish to see may see at once. Why is this? Though acquaintances fill the world, how many can truly know the heart?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The moon does not exceed five; affairs do not exceed three. Now, please wash your feet and board the boat.
Turn your heads and shift your minds; skulls will lie scattered across the wilds. Let us further apply a single needle here! He struck the meditation staff once.
"The numinous tortoise has no lines of divination; the empty shell need not be bored through."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The current at Crane Gate is swift; the whirlpool of horse's milk is deep. Beyond the head of Master Lü lies Mei Mountain.
If there were one who could pass through it, they might well display their three heads and six arms. But why have you come here? Even Potalaka remains separated by the sea."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The gateway of universal penetration stands open; serenely it responds to all things. Stars are arrayed as the Milky Way hangs low; mountains and peaks rise up in misty green.
Wind, rain, snow, and frost bring the cold; people startle and chickens and dogs bark. The Tathāgata of the Radiance of the True Dharma remains, even now, outside the gate."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Linji asked the head gardener, "Where have you come from? The gardener replied, "I have come from the prefectural city to sell yellow rice.
Linji drew a line with his staff and said, "Can you sell this as well? The gardener then shouted. Linji struck him.
When the head cook arrived, Linji recounted the previous conversation. The cook said, "The head gardener did not understand the Master's meaning. Linji asked, "What about you?"
When Sheng appeared, the head cook prostrated, and Ji also struck him. The Master said: "If one can pass through the diamond ring, a single shout distinguishes guest from host;
if one can swallow the chestnut thorn, a prostration is never mistaken. Yet, when the eye at the tip of the staff is correct, those who possess merit shall be rewarded."
Suddenly picking up his staff, he said, "Is there one? Is there one? Realize it within the alms bowl.
He ascended the hall and, citing Zhaozhou’s instruction to the assembly, said: "Thirty years ago, at the hearth in the South, there was a 'no guest-host' koan.
Even until now, no one has brought it forth. The Master said, "Zhaozhou was old and lonely at heart; he turned toward the cold..."
In the ashes, shifting them eastward and westward—if you can understand this, let yourself dream as much as you wish night after night;
if you do not yet understand, you must simply continue to dream night after night.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The samādhi of the World-Honored One was not known by Kāśyapa; the samādhi of Kāśyapa was not known by Ānanda;
the samādhi of the Great Being of Perfect Penetration was not known by the youth Sudhana; the samādhi of the youth Sudhana was not known by the elder Candracchattra.
With a roar and a shout, the spirits of ten thousand people were drained. Whose samādhi is this? (After a long pause: "As expected."
[The Master] did not speak.

On the occasion of the summer retreat’s conclusion (*jie-xia*), he ascended the hall and said: "Throughout the nine months of summer, there was no talk of 'surpassing the Buddhas and patriarchs,' nor did I cast the worldly nets of dust before you.
Today, as the retreat concludes, I untie my sackcloth bag and, relying solely upon this ready-made case, strike the flower vase with my staff."
He said: "I thought it was I who owed you; it turns out you owe me. Ascending the hall, he said:
"When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is like losing one's parents. A dull bird flies against the wind. When the Great Matter has been clarified, it is like losing one's parents.
A fish striking the water suffers a headache. Nevertheless, were it not for the wild geese arriving last night, how could one see the autumn at the sea gate?"
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: A monk asked Muzhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Muzhou said, "A team of monks comes; a team of monks goes. The Master said, "A team of monks comes; a team of monks goes.
Breaking through Muzhou’s barrier, there is not an inch of ground left in the great earth."
The Abbot ascends the hall for the ritual of receiving offerings: "When departing, the scorching heat was intense; returning now, mid-autumn has passed.
Sitting upon a flat rock amidst the woods, I cannot help but laugh heartily. I do not laugh at Yangshan planting his spade and crossing his hands, nor do I laugh at Dizang sowing rice in the fields."
"Everyone has two measures of superior rice; yet they laugh at those who starve to death by their own rice baskets.
He ascended the hall and raised the teaching, saying: "As I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light; as you briefly raise your mind, worldly toil first arises.
The hundreds of thousands of great assemblies on Vulture Peak did not understand how to be guests, thus troubling the host. With his staff, he leaned it against [the wall].
The Zen Seat says: "A single staff is supported by two people.
Compiled by the disciple Yuankai from the *Recorded Sayings* of the Abbot of Dazhong Chan Temple at Yuelin in Qingyuan Prefecture.
The three gates: the Great Way has no path, yet the tracks have long been established; liberation has no door, yet the barriers are already closed. (He lets out a shout.
The winds and clouds of the six directions arise with every step.

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of the youth Sudhana. Before the Vairocana Pavilion, Sudhana said, "This is the dwelling place of those who have realized emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Maitreya Bodhisattva snapped his fingers, making a sound, whereupon the doors of the pavilion opened;
he commanded Sudhana to enter, and once he had entered, the doors closed again. The Master said, "In this place, it is easy to see Maitreya, but difficult to see Sudhana."
Maitreya again snapped his fingers and said, "Arise! Such is the nature of reality (dharmatā). The Master said, "It is easy to see Sudhana here;

it is difficult to see Maitreya. Whether emerging or entering, what is easy to see and what is difficult to see—if one does not sleep in the same bed, how can one know that the lining of the quilt has worn through?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Patriarch did not come from the West; Shaolin has no secret technique. In Jiangnan and the two Zhe regions, spring is cold and autumn is hot—mistaken!
The Buddha-dharma pervades the world, yet when discussing the profound mystery, the mouth does not open. This is the pillar; that is the incense altar—mistaken!
Even if you were to realize it with perfect clarity, you would still be unable to avoid taking the mistaken for the correct."
When Master Yǎnxī of Jìngcí took up his post in the world, he was entrusted with the robe. The robe of faith is not transmitted; yet even a thief has nothing empty-handed.
The Dharma spreads throughout the world, like a target that draws an arrow. But tell me: at that time, who among those at Wǔfēng hit the mark? A thousand hearings are not equal to one seeing.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Touzi, “What is the Ten-Body Tamer? Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood there.
The monk asked again, “How far apart are the ordinary and the sage? Touzi likewise descended from his meditation seat and stood there.

The Master said: “A poor household is not yet truly poor; a poor road brings one to despair. Twice he descended from the meditation seat and stood there—old age does not take pride in physical strength.”

A shout. Entering the hall on the Winter Solstice: There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; the more one looks up at it, the higher it rises. Formless, it is fundamentally solitary; the more one drills into it, the firmer it becomes.
It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena; when looked upon, it is right before one’s eyes. It does not wither along with the four seasons; in an instant, it is behind one’s back.
The wearing of fur is obtained from this; becoming a Buddha also depends on another.
On the first day of the New Year, ascending the hall: the first phrase is the "Chapter One: Opening the School and Clarifying the Meaning.
The final phrase is "Twenty-five autumns, the long tolling of the evening bell. The middle phrase is: "The Buddhas appear in the world; the Patriarchs come from the West; throughout the land..."
The old monk has no place to open his mouth. The government has fixed regulations, yet it permits private agreements among the people.

(He strikes the meditation staff once. He thanks the head seat and ascends the hall. Meeting fellow travelers on the road, they pass each other shoulder-to-shoulder for a lifetime; their studies are complete.
The ancients built a single-plank bridge at the edge of the Diamond Ocean, reaching all the way to the Suyama Heaven. How many people are there?
"Come this way! A stumble in hand or foot—this alone is difficult to deceive those who are 'in the know.

Who is it that is 'in the know'? *Tut!* Ascending the hall: No Maitreya above in heaven; no Maitreya below in earth. To open one's mouth is as heavy as a thousand catties; the skin on one's face is three inches thick.
The old woman east of the city covers her face with her hands; the numinous tortoise drags its tail, and as it brushes away the tracks, new tracks arise."
Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat: Restraining the feet to protect living beings, beneath one’s heels, those begging for their lives are in a state of chaotic turmoil.
To seek realization within a fixed period, people are buried alive on level ground by the tens of thousands.

the golden duck's incense has faded and the night-watch is long. Deeply silent, moss of purple hue grows upon the jade palace; in the high void there is a moon over a thousand gates."

"When light and its object are both forgotten, what is it then? Dongshan said: "When light and its object have not yet been forgotten, what is it then?"
When light and its object are both forgotten—or even when they are not forgotten—a sharp sword kills, while a spear gives life. In times of great peace, these are utterly useless;
yet night after night, the divine light shoots out beside the Dipper.

Thundering and crashing with electric force, the seas darken the lands of Hai and Dai. Furious waves overturn and strike against the gates of heaven. The scaled fish do not know how to ride the current;
they vainly rush toward the surging waves of peach blossoms.
Praise for the Buddha’s Departure from the Mountains:

With the auspicious marks of a dragon and the refined quality of a phoenix, he departed from the royal palace; with bare elbows and tattered robes, he emerged upon the snow-capped peaks. His wisdom and vows shall surely empty all realms of existence.
The realms. Not knowing for how long the various existences have been empty, the Great Being Avalokiteśvara empties the *tathāgatagarbha*.
He establishes the great round mirror; the water falls away and the stone is revealed. The moon is bright and the clouds are pure. One gazes up at it with reverence.
The myriad capacities respond universally.

In the transcription of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the image of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), there are thirty-two manifestations of the Great Being’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Each body has thirty-two layers; this is not the Vajra’s true essence, but rather its provisional manifestation. This is the principle of non-duality.
Outside, magpies shriek and crows caw without end; the horse is the wife, and her every wish is granted.
She appears in every land, her hair disheveled and her hairpins askew, upon the banks of the Golden Sand. I bow my head in refuge.
Leakages and perils abound;

at the eastern edge of the City of Blessings, Good Wealth, we deliberated in vain. Mistakenly we entered the misty thickets and land of white birds, where waters are distant and mountains long, beyond measure.
My mind: in the end, it is difficult to express this sorrowful heart.

Vimalakīrti points at the peach and scolds the plum; the rotten seed triggers the mechanism. Words are exhausted and principles are spent; a single silence is deployed across the vast expanse, encompassing the great earth, its mountains, and rivers.
The back thunders with a roar; the Teacher of the Seven Buddhas returns in shame.
The Cloth Bag says, "Namo Ajita. Hurrying through the world, he waits for someone who has not yet arrived; let go and relax your inner belly.
He comes! He comes! *Hūḥ*. How could Mount Tai ever lack soil?
With the ninety-seven marks of a Great Man and bodies as numerous as the atoms of a hundred thousand billion worlds, the people of Tuṣita’s long embankment do not recognize him.
He rouses his spirit with a single yawn.

The Great Master Bodhidharma was a monk from the final dharma age of the Western Heaven; he came to divide this land’s first lamp. Shen Guang blew it out with a cold sigh, extinguishing it in an instant;
at the Pamir Pass, he hurriedly ascended into the darkness.
Throughout the five countries of India and the land of China to the east, the transmission of the Buddha’s Mind-essence has lacked any foundational authority to rely upon.
Lacking such a foundation, a single reed was cast across, and the great river flowed eastward.

The Fifth Patriarch’s myriad pine and cypress trees cover every mountain; having cast down his mattock, he reveals his original face once more. The two peaks stand lofty, their azure hues piercing the heavens;
though all people in the world see them, they do not see him.

The Sixth Patriarch should have remained in non-abiding; instead, he lost his way in broad daylight and stumbled at Huangmei. Though the Way has been transmitted for a thousand ages, "it is not the wind moving, nor the banner moving"—if you understand this, you are like an ant trying to shake an iron pillar.
In the painting of the Fifth Patriarch seeing off the Sixth Patriarch across the river, there is transmission and there is receiving;
favor turns into resentment. Without receiving and without transmitting, resentment resembles favor. When the boat reaches the shore, favor and resentment are severed;
throughout heaven and throughout earth, there is but one child and grandson.

Lan Zan’s chin hangs low; cold tears fill his hair with frost. The yellow tubers, roasted in the embers, possess a distinct fragrance. Summoned three times to enter the clouds, he did not rise for all three.
His descendants each established their own domains.
The Ancestor Yangqi rides a three-legged donkey, prancing on its hooves; the golden-maned lion lets out a great roar. Five peaks steep and towering touch the azure heavens;
for ten thousand generations, they have broadcasted the family’s shame.

When Jiashan saw the boatman’s lethal hand, he could not evade even a single stroke of the oar. He nodded his head, yet failed to see the one seeking the ford. Amidst the vast and boundless misty waves lies an endless regret;
though father and son are close, they are not truly kin.
For thirty years, Mazu did not lack salt or sauce in his dealings with Shigong. When that single arrow struck the midst of the pack of foxes, the great earth, mountains, rivers,
and all vegetation have, even until now, fully manifested the dynamic pivot of the arrow’s tip.
The Way and virtue of Niaoke were lofty; as his fame grew ever higher, he blew on a tuft of cloth when asked about the Buddha-dharma.
This was no ordinary, idle "cracking and pecking"—a phoenix fledged forth from an empty magpie’s nest.

The Venerable Nāgārjuna rises from the void against the stone cliff; a single stream of the Milky Way hangs suspended. Gazing greedily, there is no interruption; coming and going, one knows not its source.
The fourfold sleep.
Leaving Emei, he departs for Wutai; riding backward upon a white-faced tiger, he descends to Tiantai.
Amidst pines and upon rocks, within a dream within a dream, he calls back Governor Lüqiū to return.
Hanshan goes along the ridge to gather firewood; he carries water back by the stream. Such a person has no room for escape; even the Seven Buddhas have never been his teacher.
*The Portrait of Chan Master Focin, requested for praise by Elder Peng of Baofu.*
A thousand sages bring calamity upon their own heads; the harmonious breath of spring fills the groves. According to their capacity, those who are superior are elevated;

according to their vessel, those who are inferior are set aside. Where there is no penetration in one place, they turn heaven and earth, reviving the dead monks of the world and bringing life to the dead great earth.
This is called the wondrousness where the father does not transmit it and the son does not record it—like guarding [a treasure].
Among those who possess a thousand blessings, few are free from calamities at their heads.

Elder Qing of Shifo requested a eulogy for the source of Dongshan and the abyss of Dongjian. It is the mechanism for cutting through the current and the eye for testing men; it raises the pure and stirs up the turbid.

The earth was overturned and the heavens turned upside down. The six patriarchs of the ancestral lineage bristled their hair and snapped their fingers in reproach; the Great Image of the Three Lives stamped its feet and raised its fists.
Why should they have needed to point south? Only after the edicts of Wu and Yue were promulgated did the transmission come to be.
Eulogy for the Dharma Master Juejiang Yuanjue Wankong:

With hair unkempt and eyes piercingly sharp, he grasped the profound essence of the Tiantai school and succeeded to the prior enlightenment of Yongjia. Though he initially clung to the view of words and letters, he eventually transcended the fetters of language.
When he expounded the Great Meaning, a wind of inspiration arose among the four seats; when he investigated divergent interpretations, the hundred rivers [of doctrine] were brought into harmony.
The tide ebbs. He is a majestic *śāla* tree in the garden of the teachings, a noble wild crane amidst a flock of chickens.
Although the four quarters may not provide sufficient seating for his full deployment of skillful means, even occupying a seat among the five mountains does not belie his learning.
This is the ninth-generation descendant of Guangzhi (Guangxi). It is this single branch of the Ruo-yuan lineage that prevents it from falling into desolation.
Furthermore, he praises him as one who has sinews in his eyes and no bone in his tongue; standing tall and unique, he transcribes the torrential eloquence of the ancestral chamber of Tiantai.
Thus, his singular song resounded throughout the four quarters, transcending the marks of words and letters.

As the devas rained down flowers, those who attempted to strike the lock of his realization were scattered and driven from the assembly, while those who attained his essential meaning stood towering and majestic, beyond compare.

Moreover, he did not rely on the precious canopy of compassion or the white fly-whisk that dispels dust to pass down the family tradition; for within himself, he possessed the phoenix-glue to mend the severed strings.
Following the Dragon, he is known as King; as Director, his countenance is joyful.
He wears a *fujian* cap and loose robes, and his every step generates a wind. At the tip of his *qiongzhu* staff, a jade fly-whisk hangs high.
When attending to the Supreme Honored One, clouds follow the dragon; when examining a monk, he is like a tiger emerging from the forest. This is what is called the Way of our Teaching.
External Protection: An Inner Support within the Imperial Court.
Master Yue Tangmu, Director of the Gate, commissioned a portrait of the Master’s crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa) and requested a eulogy:

In spring, the waters fill the four marshes; In summer, the clouds abound with wondrous peaks. In autumn, the moon casts forth its brilliant radiance; In winter, the ridges show off the beauty of solitary pines.
Difficult to delineate, beyond the reach of those who understand—Yuet Tang is no ordinary acquaintance. Praised, he feels no joy; reviled, he feels no anger.
His awakening is like that of Layman Zhou:

a single circle of empty stillness, utterly devoid of conceptualization or emotion. With eyes askance and nose straight, one attempts in vain to depict his form; yet it is better not to perceive him at all, for he is the totality of sound.
As for "Color": having reviled the elder Vimalakīrti, he praised himself.
A tiger from the forest is only truly angry; a python on a ridge is only truly enraged. If there were no travelers on the road, it would ultimately not harm anyone.
The lay practitioner Wang of Leshan in Changxi, Fuzhou, sent his son Weixing to the Master to shave his head and have him paint a portrait of the Master’s crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa).
He requested a eulogy, saying:
"To hear of one's reputation is not as good as seeing one in person; to see one in person is not as good as hearing of one's reputation. These two layers of falsehood are but a pair of eyes.
"A place that does not accord with human feelings"—this phrase is to be struck down; this non-phrase is also to be struck down.
When one is in a state of total, uniform blindness, it is like forcing a dog through a wall or proving a tortoise to be a turtle. Such fabrications are hardly fit for a teacher of men.
Who knew that the saying "the same breeze blows a thousand miles away" was understood by Layman Leshan?
A gaunt, skeletal porter carrying a single load; for years he has wandered desolate through rivers and lakes. His face has been twisted beyond recognition by no one;
what idle fame could he possibly have entered into the charts of his ancestors?
The Layman Batong’an composed verses on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.

This single scripture was preached during the period of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings; it is that which "rebukes the partial and refutes the small," while "praising the great and extolling the perfect."
The Layman manifested illness in the city of Vaiśālī, hooking [the assembly] into a state beyond doubt. Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas all went to inquire after his health;
this was no ordinary act of kindness. Two thousand years later, Tong’an’s verse emerged, settling the case according to the facts.
These three segments differ, yet they are all gathered back into the primary category.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Beijian.
Master Beijian was, in his own right, a "Dew-Extinction" (Ganlu Mie) successor; he was a peer to the likes of Zhufeng An and Xiuzizhi.
Having met his ancestral teacher, Master Fozhao, his skill was perfected and his simplicity emerged, like a tiger with wings. He was *dang-dang*, *jie-jie*; *gui-gui*, *ya-ya*.
People know one thing, but do not know the second. This "ninefold entanglement" is merely self-exposure of one's own ugliness. By examining the sprouts, one discerns the field;
how could my words be false? To have no sinews in one’s eyes—this old fellow is truly being wronged.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Bashou:
The Buddhas before and after beat the poison-coating drum; Bashou’s single laugh revives those who study the Way, as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.
If there were even a single word here that either follows the current or cuts it off, this record would be the speech of a demon.
The verse states:
"Maitreya Bodhisattva was born on the eighth day of the second month;
this old man Wujixing has completely forgotten his birth month and birthday. The spring breeze and peach and plum blossoms are so abundant."
This matter is something I have spoken of to people year after year in vain.

Though the skin has been stripped away until it is black and cracked like charred wood, there still remain the scars of the axe and knife from that time. Wait until you enter the gate, and then I shall apply the final point.
Transformation: Teaching him to roll through dust and smoke wherever he goes;
once the cold arrives in the snowy courtyard, it cannot be restrained. All myriad phenomena sink into stillness. Who can enter this kind of gateway?
Entering, the footprints are clearly marked three feet deep.
A single strand of spider silk suspends the void; from a hundred billion strands, a murderous air arises, weaving a net across the zenith, nadir, and the four cardinal directions.
It is finished. Only when the net of no-outflows is cast away can the teaching proceed.
To Master Juewu, he said:

"Starting a household is as difficult as breaking one up. Once the fields and gardens are swept away, one departs from the old pass. For two thousand years, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have been cold."
A debt need not wait for a cough to be repaid all at once.
Where the water wheel of the mill turns, the water flows with a murmur; when the wheel stops, the water naturally rests. At the very end, one encounter brings knowledge of the fall.
In this place, ten parts of spring’s splendor fill the world.
At Fuxiang Pavilion, the night rain of the river city fills the terraces; the remaining red petals upon the pond cannot be stirred away. The family tradition of Maitreya has leaked out entirely.
Leakage. Good Wealth has gone south and has not yet returned.
He has sent greetings to the Venerable Qingliang Huaihai, who dwells at Wannian;
the sound of the tide suddenly turns toward Stonehead City. On the high peak of Dasheshan, listen with ears pricked: five hundred monks do not [respond].
[The assembly] gathered. He instructed [his disciples] one by one to attend to the handkerchief and the water flask as they escorted Master Mengchuang to Jingsi.
Regarding the words of Master Zhigong, he questioned Master Si about Dongjian Wuyan’s record of Dream Window. Today, Dream Window has descended from the mountain.
Go! I laugh at that Sida for having such a long tongue.
He sent this "Long Corridor Rhyme-Off" poem to Elder Tai of Guangzhou;
Old Lu once met Old Huangmei. Since they are from the same pit, there is no difference between them.
Earth. One’s private affairs must not be known to passersby.
A physician knows the nature of the disease and understands its source; who cares for the spirit when the bones are already cold? With a single piercing needle, both eyes [are healed].
Alive! Jīvaka has likely not yet received its transmission.
The clay ox hides in the west and enters the sea gate; until this very day, the ten thousand phenomena are at rest. The hundred birds do not come, yet spring comes of itself.
Old age. The thatched gate still faces the eastern mountain.

Having died the great death, one enters every door and household, staking one's very life; unaware, the whole body falls over a precipice, and all of space throughout the ten directions perishes together.
Extinction. The eight facets of the *linglong* reveal a corpse.
Sending off the cat—great compassion sows small spots. The capacity for soft blood is also idle. Head and tail are straight; the pupils...
Correct. One does not realize that the mountain atop one's own house has slipped away.
With cold rags, not even a needle-point is exposed as they are patched layer upon layer; when the seams are joined, one must investigate them closely. Let it go—there is neither needle nor patch.
Abiding there, with frozen clouds hanging to the ground, he carries it upon one shoulder.
He establishes the Hall of Water and Land;

within the great ocean of awakening, a single bubble arises. The waves and currents of the ten realms of existence do not cease for a moment. Returning to the root and restoring the source, emptiness is awakening.
The sea; the wind, moon, and rain have just cleared within the hall.
From the depths of his storehouse, he unleashes a barrage of foul words at the door, seeking only one who does not recognize his kindness. The affairs of two thousand years cannot be concealed.
It covers; as soon as it moves, it follows behind the person's heels.

It shows that even if one serves [the master] with all one’s might, if one does not contemplate the gate of the face, one will not sever it. Let it go and buy new straw sandals from the start. Where there is a path, do not walk; where there is no path, do not hesitate.
Entering, he looks after his family as they fall over a precipice.
In this hermitage, how many kalpas of worldly ash have been seen to fly? The old house remains as before, facing the setting sun; it pervades all four great continents.
The journey ends, returning once more to this very place.

At the mountain pass where the woodcutter’s hut sells firewood for no price, he returns from Lingnan; yet his children and grandchildren still remain amidst the green mists. There, holding trees and binding thatch, they maintain the household.
Separate! Part from it! Thorny brambles entangle one's robes.

To send someone traveling afar—there is a heaven to the south and Five Terraces to the north. Take this clearly to heart; do not doubt or speculate. Once the pivot of the discourse is lost, one knows it no more.
"Please give me three coins to buy straw sandals.

On the branches and beneath the leaves of the walnut tree, there is no place to hide. Standing alone and without support, I have not yet encountered my match. With one blow, my entire body is reduced to powder."
Shattered. Only when it can no longer be gathered up does its fragrance begin to spread.

A Japanese monk and a Hu monk named Bìguān sent this to the Great Liáng; it is the "Method for Delivering the Living and the Dead" transmitted solely through direct succession. To this day, this art pervades all under heaven.
Downward! Crossing seas and climbing mountains, one toils in vain.

Furthermore, a great vessel floats through the void, riding the waves; though the eye upon the crown of the head exists, it has never been opened. Turning the body within the tiger’s mouth of the Southern Mountain.
He departed. A calamity was born in Japan.
He sent attendant Zuda to summon him, yet [the master] never left his side. Generally speaking, meeting once is difficult enough; returning with knitted brows and gnashing teeth is even harder.
One day, he bitterly reviled the National Teacher of Nanpōzan, saying:
"A withered skull! I carry one 'self' as a single load;
I alone pack this burden. I know not how many wombs I have entered and exited. The Iron Ring Mountains are as high as peaks."
Granted. Smash the skull and go back!
Building a shrine while illness pursues you one after another is already too late. You have locked away this empty shrine for a long time; tomorrow at the foot of Mount Beimang—
Briefly: After the fire, who gathered the eyebrows from beneath their eyes?
A scion of Bāirán has suddenly sprouted where the cliffs and rocks split apart; unlike the pines and cypresses that grow long brushing the clouds, these towering trees have not a single idle branch.
Leaves: when the fruit falls, the grove is fragrant. Advancing toward the Moon Pavilion, the cassia orb shines solitary and bright;
the azure sky is vast. The curtain is rolled back as the pure light enters the seat with a chill. What is this luminous reality that people do not perceive?
The mat is spread; again, the flower-shadow shifts onto the balustrade.
To show this, Master Zishou said to the supervisor Huiyi:
"One arises from one; do not cling to them. Turn your face toward the south and look at the Big Dipper. Thus he thoroughly investigated and exposed the hidden essence of Mount Moshan.

with hands raised high, he washes his stones by the bamboo stream and pierces the cliffs, solitary and vast. Following the current and cutting it off, he deceives himself; he has exhausted his search until he no longer knows the source. The wind-stirred branches—
Rain-soaked leaves rustle in the wind;
the mountain elder repeatedly displays his spring-like countenance. With snow filling his hair from top to bottom, he bears no signs of aging. Lofty and solitary, few venture to visit him.
The blade and the tweezers respond to the mind as they move through the hands, yet they do not deviate by even a hair’s breadth. When both mind and hand have vanished, one penetrates everywhere.
Plucking a single strand of beard and snapping a single pair of tweezers—some aspects are identical, while others are not.
On a day of restoring antiquity, I asked the Master about the depths of his art. He turned the divination board and laughed heartily: "Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon this long ago;
yet until this very day, he has not attained its wondrous essence."

Shi Yi Shangren’s *Xuedou Wuchang Xisun* (The Suddenness of Impermanence at Xuedou) contains the details of entering the gate: the final pivot of letting go from the precipice. Each pivot and each pivot-point are self-deceptive;
by the streamside there is a stone tortoise.
Receiving guests as they come and go in a bustling flurry— who among those monks has a forehead? Sitting upon a red-hot iron bed and swallowing molten iron—
these are the descendants of Shitou and Nanyue.

The six openings of the damaged window are empty and bright, requiring no cultivation; there is a reason for the seven holes and eight apertures. Frost, wind, sleet, and snow enter from every direction;
even one who is not a man of sorrow is moved to grief.
The field of arms where history unfolds is the foundation of peace. Cease comparing heroes with respect to right and wrong. Ask the wind and moon across the vast sky:
they have never known the Zhou, Qin, Han, or Wei.
Pity that the incense burner lacks beast-charcoal and one sits without felt mats; these three pieces of firewood are simply natural.
Do not lightly let out the family’s private shame, for it would surely scorch the earth and smoke the heavens.
Revealing the Perfect Mirror: profound, pure, and luminous;
vast as heaven and broad as earth. This one perfect mirror encompasses the four infinities of light, darkness, form, and space.
This is the Wayman’s enjoyment prior to birth—the eye upon the crown of the Patriarch Baizhang.

Lanting’s four modes of deportment traverse lofty mountains and steep ridges. He loses his footing and kicks over an ancient well; his entire body is waves and billows—what need is there for three pauses and four requests?
He resided in an ancient temple during the Jin Dynasty. Without rice, salt, or vinegar, he went begging from all his neighbors every year more than three hundred and sixty times.
Sitting amidst lush forests and tall bamboos, where lofty integrity and hollow sincerity filled his sight, everyone there was indeed his own descendant. — Xiangyan’s Mouth.

Mute-tongued and bald-headed, he reclines amidst the winding streams of the Nine-Bend Cup. At Green Source, the Bai family’s fragrance has ripened; with three cups, they take their place upon the earth beneath the canopy of heaven, no longer distinguishing east from west or south from north.
Potalaka’s three phrases, Potalaka’s single path: coming and going, one bumps into the head of the great turtle; countless winds and waves.
Potalaka’s one mystery: pulling back the sleeve and rolling up the fist, one knocks off the nostrils. "Heaven! Heaven!"

Potalaka is uniquely wondrous; no one can reach it. Yet, eating, dressing, defecating, and urinating—these small matters of daily life constitute the entry into the Patriarchs’ Hall for the Venerable Wujie of Jingci.
Breaking through the Jianmen Pass, thorns and brambles grow everywhere; there is nowhere to be arranged. The hall is high, attached to the Southern Pole.
Holding up the spirit tablet, he said: "To see Master Wujie here is not yet enough;

for after the Dharma Master Xianyun of Lower Tianzhu entered the tomb in nirvana, his marks of a great man could not be contained within the void of the ten directions. A single sheet of idle clouds rolls back again."
Relax. A thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks display a chilling hue. What is it like when one departs in this very manner? The earth is vast and people are few;
those who meet are rare.
Master Ling, light the fire.
The one spiritual true nature does not rely on a womb; it emerges suddenly, massing here, surging eastward and then vanishing westward.
Like sparks flying and thunder rushing, one cannot catch up with it. Yet there is still more beyond this. Master Lingzang, last night the western wind shook the forest trees;
across a thousand mountains and ten thousand peaks, the *bèiyè* (sacred leaves) were turned over.
If the Assistant Abbot Huo (the novice Tie-niu) calls it "Suchness" (*tathatā*), he has already altered it.
Suchness does not change; it is fully manifest. The suchness of the sage and the suchness of the ordinary person are one suchness, without a second suchness.
It is the suchness of the Assistant Abbot, yet not [merely] the suchness of the Assistant Abbot. If it were produced from suchness, suchness would originally not exist.

If it arises, it is like its cessation; as it was originally, so it does not cease. Following the "Iron Ox" mechanism of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one is blown by the karmic winds amidst a swirling mass of foul smoke.

The Master of Huazhu entered the very marrow, piercing through the barrier of birth and death. He emerged from the views of existence and non-existence and shattered empty space; where could he possibly tread? It is within a heap of cold ashes.
The shadow is exposed while the body is hidden within the seamless stupa; though there are ten thousand transformations and a thousand changes, these too are the wheel-ruts of the Qin era.
The Fire Abbot’s depth is bottomless and shoreless; white waves overturn the void as he stands firm, shaking the City of Nirvana. The fire-serpent drills through the ruined wall.
The Brahmin Jvalanāmukha nodded his head, yet Sumerudīpa did not recognize it. Master Yuan found the source of the Way;
like a thirsty deer rushing toward a mirage, he pursued its origin. Master [Xuefeng] found no source in the Way; like one fleeing from a shadow in the midday sun, he sought its trace. This is—
As for its source: it does not admit of expedient means. Upon level ground, waves surge a thousand fathoms high; within the void, stars fly and sparks fly.

Master Tong’s *huozong* (fire-lineage) and *shetong* (penetration of speech)—though mountains and passes may be ten thousandfold, a single phrase does not reach them. Smash through the great void, and you shall enter.
The furnace and bellows of the Southern Mountain dwell within tiger dens and demon palaces. The iron pot for brewing tea is not the same as the cauldron;
the practitioner is pure and clear, the fire is pure and clear—the practitioner does not enter nirvana, but dies right here. The Southern Mountain shall transform you; [the Master] threw it down.

*The Biography of Zen Master Dajian of Lingyin*.
The Master’s name was Puji; he styled himself Dachu. He was the son of the Zhang family of Liuzhao in Fenghua, Siming.

His father was Youchong and his mother was Lady Yu, both of whom possessed virtuous conduct. In their daily lives, they lived on water and clouds and wore straw sandals; they constantly prayed for the birth of an excellent son.

Beyond his duties as a Confucian scholar and his responsibilities for the family, he further aspired to study Buddhism and leave the household life, believing that through this, goodness could be extended to his kin.
Consequently, three sons were born; the Master was the youngest. From childhood, he was grave and steady; even among his peers, he alone rarely spoke or smiled.

With his hair tied in a topknot, he drifted between the local schools; yet he lacked any intention for worldly affairs. Upon seeing Buddhist scriptures, he would sit upright and delve into their exegesis, forgetting even to rest.
When his parents saw this, they said, "Of our three sons, it was our original wish that at least one should leave the household life."
At the age of nineteen, he followed Master Wenxian of Xianglin Temple to shave his head and receive full ordination. Master Wenxian directed him to enter the teachings through the Vinaya;

consequently, he registered at Huxin in the prefecture to investigate the doctrines of what is permitted and what is prohibited. Later, carrying his book-bundle to Chicheng, he gained a deeper understanding of the principle of the inherent nature.
One day, he suddenly exclaimed: "The observance and violation of precepts merely constrain the body, while scholastic study is fragmented and disjointed."

"How can one transcend birth and death? Thinking thus, he left the teachings and entered into meditation. He stayed briefly at Ruiyan (Auspicious Rock) and He’u (Lotus Hut), after which he went to Tiantong to see Wuyuan.

There, he lived in a single room with profound stability; he joined the assembly but did not leave the Sangha hall. Within his state of stillness and concentration, he attained illumination, such that his speech and silence were unhindered.
During a session in the room, Wuyuan raised the koan: "The phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning are like a vine leaning against a tree."
The Master said, "Cutting through nails and slicing through iron. Yong said, "Huishan laughed heartily; what does that mean? The Master said, "A single nail driven into wood.
Yong took his bowl and was ordered to serve in the Attendant’s Office. Yong declined the position and went instead to Yujia. At that time, Chan Master Fozhao was living in retirement at Dong’an;
upon seeing Yong, he recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and directed him to go to Nengren in Yue to see Zeweng.
The Old Man asked, "Where are you from, Senior? The Master replied, "Fenghua. The Old Man said, "Do you recognize Hanzhuo the Bag-Man? The Master lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*).
The Old Man snatched away the sitting cloth and struck him. At that moment, the Master was suddenly liberated. He immediately responded, saying, "Today I have offended the Master;
I shall remain here for a long time. Later, he traveled extensively through various regions. Songyuan Kengtang and Chidun Xi... [acknowledged him].
The reclusive monk Ankong (Wuzheng) entered the gates of various elders; wherever the dragons and elephants trod, he moved with them, engaging in exchanges that were both spirited and intimate.

Furthermore, he crossed the Huai River and traveled to the Xiang River to pay homage at the stupas of the successive patriarchs. Shortly thereafter, when Zhe’ou moved to Zhongfu, he invited the Master to accompany him.
Later, by imperial decree, [Zhe’ou] was transferred to Tiantong, where the Master served as the Librarian (Zhizang). In the third month of the tenth year of the Jiading era.
When the seat at Miaosheng was vacant, the Provincial Governor summoned all the Chan masters for an assembly; the Master was chosen for this honor.
He offered incense in homage to Zeweng, commemorating the realization he had attained. Subsequently, he moved through eight successive appointments:
Putuo, Yuelin, Baoyuan of Xiu, Daci of Ningbo, Tianzhang of Yue, Jingci of the Capital, and Lingyin. Regarding his tenure at Yuelin, it was [endowed] by the Chancellor...
When the late Prime Minister, the Duke of Zhongxian, admired his spiritual worth, he invited him for an audience and promoted him to Daci Temple;
when the Gonghui Gong, Tongzhi, submitted a memorial on his behalf, an imperial edict was issued and he was promoted to Jingci Temple;

when Zhao Dazai, the Metropolitan Governor, submitted a memorial, he was summoned from the seclusion of Roushou and promoted to Lingyin Temple—this was a promotion in accordance with the established order. After residing there for two years, because...

He urgently requested to retire. The assembly closed their ranks and earnestly entreated him to remain. On the auspicious first day of the lunar month, he ascended the hall to offer blessings for the Emperor;

after descending from his seat, the monks followed him to the abbot’s quarters. They were delighted that he had recovered. Suddenly, the Master delivered a discourse, exhorting them with such fervor and intensity that it was unlike anything he had said before.
The assembly marveled at this. At dawn on the eighth day, leaning back against his couch, he composedly wrote a letter of parting to his disciples.
The eminent protectors of the Dharma of the court addressed the assembly, saying, "I am now departing.

Regarding the rites for his final passage, they were ordered to be conducted identically to those for ordinary monks—neither elaborate nor extravagant—and that the defects of later sectarian practices must not be followed, lest they invite the derision of the wise.
After the cremation, the remaining ashes were collected and cast into the river. Then, he wrote this verse: "Earth, water, fire, and wind were foretold by the Buddhas of old; In cold ashes..."

There were no relics within the funeral pyre; they were swept away into the white surging waves of the Yangtze River. For ten thousand ages, this is the foremost principle. The assembly wept and requested his final verse.
The Master smiled and said, "I still regret it being too little. He then wrote: "Coming, there is no place of origin; departing, there is no destination.
Space bursts asunder, and the mountains and peaks break into dance. Having cast down his brush, he passed away after a short while. His body was cremated, and [relics] were obtained.

The relics were five-colored, like beans in size. His disciples, wishing to honor his instructions for water burial, were moved by the former Magistrate Zhao, who specially donated gold and silk to commission the construction of a stupa.
Thus, the stupa was erected at the western foot of the temple, to the left of Master Tong’s stupa.
The first day of the eighteenth [lunar] month in the first year of the Baoyu era. He was seventy-five years of age and fifty-six years since his ordination.

His disciples numbered more than seventy; those who succeeded him in the Dharma appeared one after another. The Master possessed a solitary and firm character, and his countenance was stern and severe.

His marvelous turning of the wheel according to the occasion was such that even a pearl could not withstand his touch. When facing affairs, his discernment was as firm as a mountain that might yet be uprooted.
Once he had dedicated his person to the Way, whether worldly conditions were adverse or favorable, nothing was sufficient to cause him to waver or be disturbed.

Whether acting for himself or for others, he applied this same principle in all his conduct. Students found his severity and rigor difficult to approach; yet after a long time, they came to feel a deep sense of affection and attachment toward him.
"Be patient and depart. This direct pointing is urgent. It is like the cup of a sorcerer’s household: those who drink from it will surely die;
it is like the prescription of a skilled physician: those who take it will surely live. When Old Man Zhe was about to pass away, he said to his disciples:
'The Elder Jie of Yue-lin knows where my tongue falls; you may have him collate my recorded sayings. Now, these words of Fo-xin are being circulated."
This was determined by the Master of the World. He set aside his own surplus to provide for the permanent endowment of the monastery, regarding it as lightly as tossing a pebble.

He repaired deficiencies and restored what was ruined, acting according to what was appropriate for the time. During his tenure at Jingci Monastery, he observed the topography and orientation of the site, noting that the left side was elevated while the right was low.
He then emptied his alms bowl and bag and erected a pavilion on the southeast side. By housing the Buddhas of the Three Ages there, he further enhanced the splendor of the lake and mountains.

When the Emperor heard of this, he bestowed generous rewards upon him. He even personally inscribed the imperial calligraphy for two plaques—“Zhengbianzhi Ge” (Pavilion of Universal Knowledge) and “Huayan Fajie” (Avataṃsaka Dharma-realm)—to be displayed there, which shone with brilliant beauty.
While residing at the mountain, he remained in seclusion, maintaining a single-minded discipline as pure as ice and gall, his quarters being simple and austere.
However, it is like a traveler’s inn; one regards those who serve as mere passersby. When the master sends them out on errands, he does not employ them for any labor at all.
How can this be compared to those who have stolen titles and positions, acting with arrogance and haughty looks?
Therefore, the monks of the rivers and lakes think of this even after a long time. In the winter of the year *Bao Yu* *Yi Mao*, while I was residing at Ciyun, his son Yongji came to visit.
I have recounted the Master’s life from beginning to end; as it accords with what I had previously heard, I have arranged it into a systematic account.

This record is prepared for the perusal of the eminent gentlemen of the present age, so that it may be inscribed in a stele to endure for posterity. As for the "Discourse on the Eight Assemblies," the Master, at the time of his passing, took it up and cast it into the fire.
What is currently in circulation consists of various monastics who have transmitted and recited these teachings, compiling them into a single volume to be shown to future generations.

It is said: On the eve of the full moon in the first month of the fourth year of the Baoyu era, at the Great Compassion Mountain, Jiaozhong Baoguo Chan Temple in Qingyuan Prefecture, the bhikṣu Daguan, who is under my jurisdiction, respectfully submits this formal statement regarding his special appointment as the abbot.
